0 GPU, 0 submissions, 0 training. Every shell carried CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" under nice -n 10 while T007's fold held the card.
Read-only on the repo except this file.
Written incrementally: sections appear in the order they were established.
Every claim is marked READ (quoted from a primary page or file), MEASURED (computed here, command given in Appendix A), or INFERRED (an estimate with its model stated).
A bracket is never a measurement and is never written as one.

What can honestly be said about our rerun runtime

Nothing else exists.

### 1.2 A fourth instrument nobody had used: the notebook logs carry timestamps
outputs/t039/v16_log/rsna-knee-submit.log and outputs/t040/v1_log/rsna-knee-efficiency.log are Kaggle's JSON logs, and every stdout line carries a time field in seconds since kernel start.
The kernel prints a line at the start and end of each bag layout pass, so each pass is directly timed on the real T4.
Three passes exist:

The two cold passes differ only in forward count, so their difference isolates the marginal cost of a forward unit with warmup and reads cancelling:
> MEASURED: 0.0653 s per study per member-view unit on a Kaggle T4.

### 1.3 The cross-check that makes this a measurement and not a model
Fit T = a + b·u to datapoints A and B (the two with real wall clocks), using B's 73 min midpoint:
> MEASURED: T(u) ≈ 25.2 min + 1.329 min per forward unit, i.e.
> 0.0613 s per study per unit at ~1300 test studies.
> Propagating B's 68–78 min interval gives 0.0547 – 0.0679 s/study/unit.

The log-derived 0.0653 sits inside the wall-clock-derived 0.0547–0.0679. These are two genuinely independent instruments — one is a 3-study notebook run timed by Kaggle's own logger, the other is two submissions timed by a poller against ~1300 hidden studies — and they agree on the marginal cost of a member-view to within 6 %.
That is the strongest runtime statement this board has.
(Honesty note: the "warmup ≈ 10.79 s implied by both logs" figure I first computed is an algebraic identity of the three-pass fit, not an independent check, and is therefore not quoted as evidence.
The 0.0653-vs-0.0613 agreement is the real check.)
### 1.4 Is the deployed 22-member rerun's runtime known?
No — but it is now bounded far better than 90.5–264.7
The fitted model predicts the deployed config at
> INFERRED: 25.2 + 1.329 × 66 = 113 min submit→terminal, of which
> 93 min is GPU forwards (1300 × 66 × 0.0653 / 60, the log-derived rate).
113 min sits inside the observed 90.5–264.7 min bracket, which is a consistency check the bracket can pass but not sharpen.
The deployed rerun's runtime is still not measured. What changed is that the honest statement is no longer "somewhere between 1.5 h and 4.4 h";
it is "a fitted 113 min from two agreeing instruments, consistent with the only observation we have".
### 1.5 The 1 + M·V budget model, checked — and lane 7 §3.4 corrected
src/tta.py:324 defines budget_minutes(members, views) = 1.0 + members × views, documented as an upper bound derived from T009's "~6 min at 5 members, ~2 min at
Checked against everything above:
claim
verdict
slope 1.0 min per member-view
MEASURED at 1.329 min/unit. The model is 24 % optimistic on the slope, not conservative.
Its "upper bound" docstring is wrong in sign.
intercept 1.0 min
MEASURED at ~25 min in the submit→terminal metric.
How much of that 25 min is queue and scoring rather than notebook time is not established (see §1.6).
the model ignores layouts
The kernel already prints × ~N for the extra pass(es);
the layouts partition members, so (1 + M·V) is the wrong shape and 1 + Σ_layouts (M_layout × V) is right.
At the deployed config both happen to give 67.
lane 7 §3.4: "the model under-predicts by 2× in practice"

This is not right as stated. Its "measured ~134 min" is 67 × 2 layout passes, which is the kernel's own printed prediction, not a measurement — the 2× is the layout multiplier the kernel already applies, not a modelling error.
The real error is the 1.33× slope error in §1.5 row 1.
Lane 7's conclusion (the Raptor arm fits inside 9 h) survives;
its reasoning should not be reused.
T009's "~6 min at five members" cannot be reconciled with 0.0653 s/study/unit (five members at one view is 5 units ⇒ ~7 min of forwards, which actually fits;
"~2 min at one member" ⇒ 1.4 min of forwards, which also fits).
T009 is consistent with the new rate, and the intercept it inferred (~1 min) is the part that was wrong, because T009 was reading notebook time and not submit→terminal time.
That is the same ambiguity §1.6 records.
### 1.6 Per-submission runtime is still not readable without a browser — verified, not assumed
T040's claim was re-tested rather than inherited.
Four checks, all negative:

ApiSubmission (kagglesdk/competitions/types/competition_api_service.py:4636) — READ, complete attribute list: ref, total_bytes, date, description, error_description, file_name, public_score, private_score, status, submitted_by, submitted_by_ref, team_name, url.
No runtime field.
ApiGetSubmissionRequest takes only ref and returns the same object.
ApiKernelMetadata (kagglesdk/kernels/types/kernels_api_service.py:960) — READ: last_run_time is a timestamp, not a duration, and there is no duration field.
The only time-like quantity in the kernels service is total_time_allowed, which is a cap, not a measurement.
Empirical: kaggle kernels list --user bhavishnithinr --csv reports lastRunTime 2026-09-02 05:15:56 for rsna-knee-efficiency, and the submission was made at 05:18:36 and went terminal at 05:45:07.
lastRunTime therefore tracks the visible 3-study version run only and is not touched by the scored rerun.
kaggle kernels status returns a status string and nothing else.
kaggle kernels output has no version-selecting flag beyond owner/kernel/version for versions we can enumerate, and the rerun is not one of them.
Settled: no competitor-reachable API exposes the scored rerun's runtime. This is now checked at the SDK-schema level and empirically, and should not be re-searched.
### 1.7 What the unused hours actually amount to
The cap is 9 h = 540 min of notebook run time (READ, lane 0: "GPU Notebook <= 9 hours run-time").
Our notebook portion is at most the 113 min of §1.4 and is smaller by however much of the 25 min intercept is Kaggle-side queue and scoring.
> INFERRED: at least 540 − 113 = 427 min of unused notebook budget, and
> 1.329 min buys one forward unit per study.
So ≈ 320 more units/study are
> affordable — the deployed 66 could become ≈ 380, a 5.8× increase in forward
> work, with zero training GPU.
A timeout forfeits the submission, so a real config should target roughly half the cap.
At 270 min the budget is ≈ 185 units/study, 2.8× the deployed 66.
The inference-only levers, ranked
Costs are in forward units per study (one member scoring one view of one bag) and converted at the §1.3 rate of 1.329 min per unit.
The deployed config is 66 units ⇒ ~113 min;
the working ceiling is ~185 units at half the 9 h cap.
### 2.0 First, a free measurement that kills the obvious lever
outputs/t039/dumps/ holds 120 per-view prediction CSVs — all 12 --adjacent members × {id, crop, bright, cropX, brightX} × {oof, gold}, written by T039 rule 2.
Nobody had used them to measure the view return curve.
Done here with no GPU (script in Appendix A):
views
gold-58 AUC (12 adj. members)
Δ, paired 95 %
OOF rho, 4,349 studies
Δ, paired 95 %
id,crop
id,crop,bright (deployed)
MEASURED.
The view curve has already turned over. The second view resolves positive on the 4,349-study instrument;
the third view resolves negative, its band excluding zero.
Gold cannot resolve either step, consistent with its ±0.0044–0.0101 paired band.
Two consequences, and they are the main result of Half A:
"More TTA views" is dead as a lever. A fourth view of the same kind is being proposed onto a curve whose third step is already measurably negative.
This is a null result and it was free — no GPU, no submission.

This is not licence to drop bright. T003 pre-registered that per-view dumps may be opened only when the bundle fails, precisely because "picking a view set after seeing per-view numbers is the move that cost 0.008 at P2".
The measurement above is research under T047 rule 3 (nothing is adopted).
A task to drop bright would have to register its rule first, and its expected LB value is about −0.0005 rho × the 0.74 TTA transfer ratio ≈ +0.0004 LB, i.e. below what the LB can show.
Not worth a submission.
### 2.1 The one lever with real headroom: slice density at inference
MEASURED, data/manifest.csv, 13,221 series: the corpus holds a mean of 34.8 slices per series (median 30, p90 40).
src/dicom_io.py:480 picks np.linspace(0, len(order)-1, max_slices) — evenly spaced, deterministic, no randomness.
So at the deployed --slices 12:
--slices
mean slices used
share of all slices seen
series fully consumed
12 (deployed)

Two thirds of every series is currently discarded at inference. Unlike crop and bright, which re-present the same pixels through a mild transform, denser sampling supplies pixels the model has never been shown.
That is why the flat view curve in §2.0 does not predict this lever's return.
It is mechanically free of code risk on our members — three checks, all READ:

- KneeMIL.forward only enforces bag-length divisibility inside the SliceSequenceHead branch, and all 22 checkpoints carry seq_head False or absent (MEASURED, torch.load over outputs/ckpt22/.pt), so self.seq is None and no length check runs.
- The slot position fed to the model is pos[:n_real] = linspace(0, 1, n_real) (src/dataset.py:138) — normalised, so bag-length invariant.
- Both pooling heads are a masked softmax over the slice axis (src/model.py:30, :79) — length-agnostic.
Caveats, stated because they are real. The model was trained at 12 slots, so this is a train/test bag-length mismatch;
the kernel's own comment warns that attention pooling "just scores a differently-shaped study".

And for the 12 --adjacent members the gain is smaller than the table suggests: 2.5D already decodes i−1, i, i+1 around each of the 12 picks, so those members' pixel coverage is already near-complete even though they still get only 12 attention slots.
The 10 non-adjacent members are the ones literally seeing 34.5 %.
Cost. Doubling slices doubles the bag and so doubles the forward units: 66 → 132 units ⇒ ~175 min, comfortably inside 9 h.
T028's --slices 36 OOM is not a constraint here: it was measured with a backward pass on the local 8 GiB card, and inference on a 16 GiB T4 carries no gradients.
INSTRUMENT, and it is cheap. Re-dump one member at --slices 24 over gold-58 and over one fold's 869-study OOF block, then compare against the same member's existing id dumps.
scripts/t039/dump_views.py is the harness;
it currently reads slices_per_plane and img_size from the checkpoint args (:96, :113-114), so it needs a two-line override, not a rewrite.
Bands: 869-study rho ±0.0102 and gold-58 paired ±0.0044–0.0101.
Local GPU, inference only, zero training hours — T028 measured the analogous --slices 24 probe at ~7.7 min per member over 869+58 studies.
Run at --workers 4 (the 8-worker desktop freeze of 2026-09-01).
If it survives, widen to the full OOF corpus for the ±0.0019 band before any submission is spent.
### 2.2 Higher resolution at inference
Same shape of argument as §2.1, weaker mechanism.
Members are trained at size=320 (MEASURED, all 22).
Raising to 384 or 448 at inference costs (size/320)² in forward FLOPs — 384 is 1.44× (66 → 95 units ⇒ ~126 min), 448 is 1.96× (~221 min).
The encoder is tf_efficientnet_b2, whose native train size is 260;
it is already being run above it.
Unlike slice density this adds no new information — it interpolates the same decoded pixels — so its only mechanism is the backbone's stride landing differently on the same anatomy.
Ranked below density for that reason. Same instrument, same cost: a one-member re-dump at img_size=384.
### 2.3 A third bag layout
Not available without new checkpoints. MEASURED: every one of the 22 members has (slices, size, seqs) = (12, 320, 1) and differs only in adjacent, so layout_of can only ever produce two groups.
MAX_LAYOUTS = 2 (rsna-knee-submit.py:85) is not the binding constraint — the pool is.
Raising the cap does nothing until a member with a third layout exists, which is training.
Ranked as not an inference-only lever at all.

The one exception is that §2.1 creates a third layout: members re-run at --slices 24 are a distinct layout from the same members at 12, so RSNA_MAX_LAYOUTS=3 would be required to ensemble both densities, and the cost is a third full data pass.
### 2.4 Overlapping windows, in the manner of the 42-window public recipe
Lane 7 records the Raptor CoAtNet at "5 slots (Sag-FS 18, Sag-noFS 14, Cor-FS 12, Cor-noFS 8, Ax 12) = 64 slices, 42 windows".
This is the same lever as §2.1, expressed in that recipe's vocabulary: their 42 three-slice windows over 64 slices is our --adjacent packing at a much higher slot count.
It is not an independent idea and should not be ranked twice.
What it adds is an existence proof from a 0.924-single-model recipe that ~3.5× our slot count is what the band above us runs at.
### 2.5 Per-label pooling over views
src/tta.py:blend already weights per view and per study and per label, but the weights are structural (a view can be undefined for a study or for a label), never fitted.
Choosing per-label view weights from data is rule-constant tuning and is prohibited (CLAUDE.md;
ROADMAP § "Explicitly not worth doing").
Ranked as blocked, not as unpromising. The only non-prohibited variant is a structural rule fixed in advance without looking at per-label numbers, and §2.0 shows there is nothing to collect anyway.
### 2.6 The unexploited asymmetry: views the armC block is trained for and the ensemble cannot use
MEASURED from the checkpoint args: the 10 armC members carry mirror = 0.5 and rotate = 25.0;
the other 12 (armb0×2, fold0-4×2) carry 0.0 for both.

tta.unmatched (src/tta.py:110) refuses a view unless every member was trained for it — if any(not float(a.get(flag, 0) or 0) ...) — so mirror, rot+ and rot- are unavailable to the 22-member ensemble solely because 12 members drag them down, not because they are invalid.
A per-member view set would let the armC block run mirror, rot+, rot- at 10 × 3 = 30 extra units ⇒ ~40 min.
The mirror is structurally far more diverse than a 0.90 centre crop, and ROADMAP explicitly permits the label-swapping mirror.
But §2.0's turned-over view curve is a poor prior, and this needs a kernel change (unmatched per member, blend per member group).
Ranked third, behind density and resolution.
INSTRUMENT: no dumps exist for these views, so it needs local inference — 10 armC members × 3 new views over their own fold blocks, ~4,349 studies.
The comparable job (5 members × 3 views over 4,349) took 27 min locally (PROGRESS, T024 screen 2), so this is ~1 h of local inference GPU and zero training hours, read against the OOF instrument.

# Lane 12 — semi-supervised and target-side levers
Research round 3 (T047), lane 12.
Written 2026-09-02 while T007 holds the GPU.
No GPU used, no submission, no repo file touched except this one.

Question. What can be extracted from the data we already hold — 4,407 studies, 24,371 series, 819,078 slices, 533 GB at /home/ade/rsna-data/, plus the ~1,300 hidden-test studies the kernel sees in one pass — without a new labeling pass and without touching a standing prohibition?
Evidence marks: READ (quoted from a primary source, file:line), MEASURED (computed here, command given in Appendix A), INFERRED (estimate with the model stated).
An unmarked number is a defect.
(sections appended incrementally as they are established)
## Verdict up front

One survivor, one partial survivor, four rejections. The lane is not null, but its single survivor is smaller and safer than the proposal that generated it, and it is not the test-time adaptation the brief opened with.

one item found: the SWA checkpoints' BatchNorm buffers were never recomputed, which is 1a's mechanism, and a second item rejected (unlabelled-corpus pseudo-labelling = self-distillation, already T035)
Test-time adaptation inside the kernel
### 1.1 Is it permitted? — READ, yes, and nothing bars it
docs/research/0902/lane0-rules-and-leaderboard.md:11-15, verbatim fragments the lane-0 session pulled through r.jina.ai:
> - "CPU Notebook <= 9 hours run-time";
"GPU Notebook <= 9 hours run-time"
> - "Internet access disabled"
> - "Freely & publicly available external data is allowed, including pre-trained models"
> - "Submission file must be named submission.csv"
The only data-handling restriction lane 0 recorded is §2.4.b, and it is about exfiltration, not about computation on the test set (docs/research/0902/lane0-rules-and-leaderboard.md:26-28):
> Data security (§2.4.b): "You agree not to transmit, duplicate, publish,
> redistribute or otherwise provide or make available the Competition Data to
> any party not participating in the Competition."
READ verdict: nothing in the rules bars adapting on the test set inside the kernel. Transduction is a standard Kaggle move and the pages read do not mention it.
(The rules were not re-fetched here;
T047's do-not-redo table forbids re-reading the rules pages, so this is lane 0's reading, not a re-derivation.)
### 1.2 The premise about mixed BatchNorm regimes is TRUE — and I can now say exactly how mixed
The brief's premise was that --grad-checkpoint double-updates BatchNorm and that the deployed 22 may therefore mix two regimes.
Both halves check out, and the shape is narrower than "the deployed 22 mix two regimes" suggests.
READ, src/train.py:481-499, the warning the code prints on every checkpointed run:
> Measured 2026-08-24 (T022), not assumed: checkpointing re-runs the forward
> during backward, and BatchNorm's running statistics are updated on both
> passes.
num_batches_tracked came back 6 after 3 steps instead of 3 [...]
> what moves is the buffer used at eval, which is what every reported score is
> computed through.
MEASURED — the doubling is real, and it is confined to encoder.blocks. Three training steps of the real model on CPU, torch 2.13.0+cu132 / timm 1.0.28 (Appendix A, bn_double.py):
--grad-checkpoint
BN counters inside encoder.blocks (67 layers)
BN counters outside (2 layers)
off

The stem (encoder.bn1) and head (encoder.bn2) sit outside the checkpointed region — scripts/smoke_test.py:3443-3444 states the same structural fact for a different reason ("timm checkpoints an efficientnet's blocks (leaving bn2 outside)").
So a checkpointed run does not have "doubled BatchNorm";
it has 67 of 69 BatchNorm layers at double the momentum applications and 2 at single, which is an internally inconsistent checkpoint, not merely a differently-calibrated one.
MEASURED — the deployed 22, audited from their own saved args and provenance (Appendix A, bn_audit3.py):

So 4 of 22 (18%) carry the split regime, and they are exactly the four the brief guessed at: the two locally trained fold-0 arms and their SWA twins.

The counters are exact — armb0.pt at epoch 4 reads 6,960 on the stem and 13,920 in the blocks, and the run's own log says train(weak)=3480 at --bs 2, i.e. 1,740 steps/epoch × 4 = 6,960 (outputs/t028/armB_fold0.log:4).
The arithmetic closes with nothing left over.
### 1.3 But the regime split is already known to be harmless, and the top of the member table is held by the doubled members
READ, PROGRESS.md:3410-3415, T022 Gate D's close-out:
> The BatchNorm double-update caution is answered. --grad-checkpoint was
> measured to update num_batches_tracked twice per step, and the registered
> question was whether that reaches the eval-time buffers.
It produced a model
> that is better than the reference, so whatever it moved, it did not break
> anything.
That caution can stop being carried as a live risk.

Gate D's numbers (PROGRESS.md:3381-3390): at --bs 2 --grad-checkpoint local fold 0 scored corpus rho 0.6451 against the archived Kaggle fold 0's 0.6336, Δ = −0.0115 against that pair's own band ±0.0112 — outside the band, in the direction of the checkpointed model being better.

MEASURED, and pointing the same way. Re-running T040's rule-1 instrument (scripts/t040/pick_member.py, 200 bootstrap draws, zero GPU, all dumps pre-existing) puts the four split-regime members in the top four places of twenty-two: armB0.swa 0.8841, armC0.swa 0.8840, armB0 0.8836, armC0 0.8828, against a 22-member floor of 0.8531.
That ranking is confounded with fold 0 and with arm B/C, and T040 says so itself, so it is not evidence that doubling helps.
It is decisive evidence that doubling is not a defect to be repaired, which is what a "statistics refresh" proposal needs to be true.
So the brief's stated reason a refresh might pay does not survive contact. The mixed regime is real, measured, and benign.
### 1.4 The real mechanism is a different one, and it is not about the test set at all
Both regimes share a property nobody has priced: the eval-time BatchNorm buffers are an exponential moving average over the last handful of training batches, not a statistic of the corpus.
At PyTorch's default momentum 0.1 the running mean has a time constant of ~10 batches;
at bs=2 with 36 slice-slots per study that is ~720 images.
Applying the update twice per step (the checkpointed regime) is algebraically an effective momentum of 1−(1−0.1)² = 0.19, i.e. ~5.3 batches ≈ 380 images.
Same expectation, roughly double the variance.
INFERRED — the model is standard BN EMA algebra;
nothing here is measured.
And 11 of the 22 members are SWA checkpoints whose BatchNorm buffers were averaged rather than recomputed. READ, src/train.py:57-63:
> Note what this does not do: BatchNorm running statistics are averaged
> along with the weights rather than recomputed over the data.
They are
> already running means over the same distribution and the tail epochs sit
> close together, so this is the cheap approximation of update_bn -- which
> would cost another pass over the loader, and the loader is the bottleneck.
> If the averaged checkpoint ever scores worse than the argmax one by more
> than noise, that approximation is the first thing to suspect.
That is torch.optim.swa_utils.update_bn's entire reason for existing, and this repo has never called it.
MEASURED — the tripwire the comment names has not fired. From the same rule-1 table, the eleven same-fold, same-held-out-block SWA-vs-argmax pairs:

The SWA checkpoints are not visibly broken by stale buffers — so this is a ceiling on the proposal, not a promise.
What it does not bound is how much better each SWA checkpoint would be against itself with recomputed buffers;
that comparison has never been made and is the only thing an experiment here would answer.
### 1.5 The two proposals, separated
1a — offline BatchNorm recalibration on our own corpus.
SURVIVES.

- Mechanism. Replace each checkpoint's EMA-tail BatchNorm buffers with a statistic computed over that fold's training studies: forward passes in train() mode with momentum=None (cumulative average), no backward, no optimizer, no labels.
Repairs three things at once — the 380-vs-720-image variance, the 67/2 internal inconsistency in the four checkpointed members, and the 11 never-recomputed SWA buffers.

- Magnitude. INFERRED, small: 0 to +0.003 on OOF AUC-vs-Sonnet per member, and less than that on the ensemble. The model is that recalibration buys at most what the SWA-vs-argmax spread above shows BN-related bookkeeping is worth on this model (max +0.0075, mean +0.0015), and ensembling 22 members averages away exactly the buffer noise this fixes.
I would not bet on the LB moving.
Anyone quoting a bigger number is quoting the literature, not this repo.
- Cost. Zero training GPU. One forward pass over ~3,500 studies per member, no backward.
PROGRESS.md:3427 records "27 minutes of local inference" for five checkpoints' extra TTA dumps (ten passes over 4,349 studies, so ~2.7 min/pass);

22 passes over ~3,500 studies is INFERRED ~50 min, call it under 2 h with reloads — interruptible, resumable, and not a training fold — it does not engage the one-fold-then-cool-down rule, which is about sustained load, though it should still go through scripts/gpu_queue.sh.
Engineering: ~40 lines (update_bn-equivalent + a re-save), plus smoke-test guards.
- Prohibition touched: NONE. It is not a labeling pass, not a flip, not a rule constant, not self-distillation.
momentum=None is not a tuned constant — it is the switch that says "average everything", the absence of a constant.
The one thing to check explicitly against docs/ROADMAP.md:480 ("Rule-labeler tuning. Settled: no constant in it is falsifiable at n=58") is that no momentum value is chosen;

- Local. CLAUDE.md is explicit: "The local GPU must not run continuously for long (operator ruling, 2026-08-26). Cap at one fold, then cool down;

never chain training jobs back-to-back", and "A fold is atomic at 1.75 h (b2) to 3.5 h (DINOv3) because train.py has no --resume." Even the truncated 11.4 h run is at least seven atomic sessions with cooldowns between them, and there is no resume machinery to make it atomic-safe.
A crash at hour 9 loses everything.
- Kaggle. 30 h/week (docs/ROADMAP.md:499).
The truncated run alone is 38% of a week;
the five folds that must follow it to be worth anything are another ~20 h at T4 rates.
It does not fit, and Kaggle kills the output of a kernel that exhausts quota (PROGRESS.md:4988).
- And the truncated run is the one with no evidence behind it. The published magnitudes for self-supervised pretraining come from 100–800-epoch schedules.
A 20-epoch contrastive run on 819k images is not a cheap version of that result;
it is a different, unevidenced thing.
### 2.4 The structural objection, which matters more than the price
The encoder is already pretrained — src/model.py:168,173-175 builds it with timm.create_model(backbone, pretrained=True, ...).

In-domain SSL has to beat a supervised ImageNet initialisation using 819k slices from 4,407 knees, which is small and highly redundant (adjacent slices of one volume are near-duplicates, so the effective sample is far below 819k).

And a cheaper, better-evidenced route to the same goal is already registered: docs/ROADMAP.md:517-522 records that external pretraining on MRNet/OAI had its third gate voided ("Pretraining can happen locally and only the resulting checkpoint need ever reach Kaggle"), and round 2's lane 8 already surveyed those sets and ranked them (docs/research/0902b/lane8-external-truth-sets.md:366, "Second-best pretraining source").
Proposing in-domain SSL would put an unevidenced 11 h run ahead of a registered, surveyed alternative.
- Prohibition touched: none. Nothing in docs/ROADMAP.md § "Explicitly not worth doing" names pretraining.
This is rejected on arithmetic and on duplication, not on a ban.
- Instrument, if anyone revives it: the 869-study held-out rho (±0.0102 on a fold-0 pair) on a fold-0 screen, and it would need to move past that band to justify the four remaining folds.
Nothing cheaper can resolve it, because the effect claimed is a training effect.

MEASURED: every one of the 4,407 studies has all three anatomical planes, and every study has at least one fluid-sensitive and at least one non-fluid-sensitive series (0 studies lack either).

So after T007, --seqs 2 has covered every (plane, family) cell in the corpus for every study. The 3,037 remaining series are the second and later entries of 2,898 cells — a second sagittal non-fat-suppressed acquisition where one has already been read, not a view the model has never seen.

Consequence — --seqs 3 is rejected. It would widen the bag from 72 to 108 slots for a 12.5% increase in distinct series that carry no new plane and no new sequence family, benefiting 1,936 of 4,407 studies (44%) unevenly, and it would cost strictly more than T007.

T007's own cost is the reference: MEASURED, git log 5dbdd25, "Epoch 1: peak_VRAM 4.25 GiB against armC's 2.20, train 29.8 min against its 16.1" — 1.85× at bag 72 — and that epoch was throttled ("at 88 C this run reports SW Thermal Slowdown: Active").
Bag 108 would be ~2.8× armC on a card that is already throttling at 2×.
